title: Ferdinand Piëch’s One-Off W-10 M5 Might Be the Wildest E39 Ever

body_markdown:
Who doesn’t love an engine swap? Whether that’s an[LS into a Miata,](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/colorado-is-where-miatas-go-to-fly/) a Honda K20 in a Lotus Elise, or[TAG F1 motor in a 911](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/classic-porsche-930-to-get-80s-f1-power/) , there’s no replacement for increased displacement.


It certainly seems to been an idea that longtime VW boss Ferdinand Piëch embraced: He once had a Golf 4Motion modified to become a 400-hp sleeper, and, as you see here, he decided that an[E39-generation BMW M5](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/bmw/m5/2002/2002-bmw-m5) would make the perfect testbed for a prototype W-10 engine.


The story of this sensational swap begins not long after Piëch (an[icon who you should absolutely know about](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1KKiqibOxoc) ) joined Volkswagen in 1993 as Chairman. Chief among his early achievements was the development of the narrow-angle VR engine range. Under Piëch, the[VR6](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/volkswagen-builds-final-vr6/) motor went from 2.9 liters up to 3.2 and then 3.6 liters. It also spawned the quirky[VR5](https://www.hagerty.com/media/lists/celebrating-50-years-of-five-cylinder-fun/) in 1997, and from there it couldn’t have taken too much imagination to figure that stitching two of these together would give you a 10-cylinder motor.


Broad Arrow


VW’s skunkworks reportedly built just three engines, with each at five liters capacity and developing some 470 hp and 437 lb-ft of torque. To put the W-10 to the test, Piëch had it fitted to a 2000 model year Carbon Black Metallic E39 BMW M5. A six-speed manual transmission was retained, but the traction control, stability control and anti-lock brakes were disabled. Custom intake ducting, ignition system, a coolant expansion tank, and a standalone ECU were all required to get the W-10 to run in the BMW.


It’s said to be super smooth with those ten cylinders sharing a common crankshaft, not to mention blisteringly fast. It packs some 80 more horses than the original V-8 M5 donor. Although the W-10 never made it beyond the prototype stage, it was an important step in the development of the[W-12](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/a-fond-farewell-to-the-bentley-w-12/) that later appeared in the VW Phaeton and Bentley Continental GT, as well as Bugatti’s[W-16](https://www.hagerty.com/media/never-stop-driving/never-stop-driving-193-two-decades-of-the-amazing-bugatti-w-16/) .


Sabine Willeke, who led the engineering team behind the W-10, confirms that the secretive, off-the-books project was estimated to have cost around €2,000,000 (around $4.5M in today’s money). Piëch used the car regularly during development, driving it on temporary plates.


Broad Arrow


What’s unclear is just exactly how far the VW boss actually drove the Franken-M5; part of the modification process included replacing the main instrument cluster with a racing Stack dashboard which had no odometer. Aside from that the black leather interior is pretty much as it left the BMW factory, down to the car phone in the center armrest.


Its current owner acquired the car around 10 years ago, having been fascinated by its history. It was road-registered in Slovakia, has been driven regularly since, and was last serviced in 2025. As a prototype, it doesn’t come with a certificate of conformity to meet various government regulations, but it is being sold with a second engine. The third unit is said to still be in Germany.


This unique vehicle is being sold at[Broad Arrow’s Zoute Concours Auction,](https://www.broadarrowauctions.com/vehicles/zt26_r0071/2000-bmw-m5-volkswagen-w10-prototype-ex-ferdinand-piech) in Belgium on October 9, and is estimated to reach €250,000-€350,000 ($285,000-$400,000). Some might say that’s a relatively small price to pay for a one-off W-10 M5, to say nothing of a fascinating chapter in the history of the VW Group.
